we are creating "yolo-twice" a tool to help individuals and teams get insights into long running claude code sessions.

The basic idea is to inspect and visualize long running conversations on the fly as they evolve and present different levels of abstraction of the transcript that allow the user to easily navigate and search the history and deep dive where they choose to. This could include interactive, time line, text search, flow graph, strechtext like semantic abstraction levels, semantic clusters etc

we can imagine a solution that has an seperate engine running that watches and indexes the users relevant  ~/.claude/* folders, transforms fil system changes into and event stream and analysis and transforms the events using local tools and eventually claude code itself. the UI could be a web UI, updated in real time. Indexing must work incrementally, so it can we stopped, resumed.

In order to keep and share the history yolo-twice shall store all state into the projects .yolo-twice folder so it can be commited with the project or gitignored.

Design principles: idempotency

claude code user could have commands in the cli like
- /yolo-twice (opens the insights UI for the current project folder, launches engine if needed )
- /yolo-twice stop ( stops the engine) 

There must be a github pages website and a readme explaining the installation as single commmand.
Our idea is to ship yolo-twice as claude plugin / mcp so first interaction is through claude cli.

We will also generate a 3 min pitch presentation, which might reuse elements of the githib page. both sould be very simple and use graphical elements as mermaid diagrams.

use open standards and protocols wherever possible. We wrote everything for claude code in this prompt but also want to extend to other coding agents like opencode in the future.

We are 4 people and want to work AI driven in parallel so a modular design would help us.

Challange our ideas. consider options and improve the idea. Search for inspiration in similar projects. Maybe we can reuse or extend working approaches.

# BaselHack Code Repo Template

This is the template repository, which makes our lives (and especially the lives of the jury) easier,
if you follow our structure.

## Explanation

Please make sure that everything, that is code related, goes into `code` directory.

If you have documentation about the code (e.g. UML Diagrams, a readme etc.), that should go into the `documentation` directory.

If you have assets (like videos, presentations etc.), this can go into the `assets` directory.

You can use the MIT license in this template. Make sure to adjust the copy right holders in the placeholder `<copyright holder>` and add every team member to it.
You are also free to choose any other license - depending on the consensus of your team.

Thanks a lot!

I found several open-source Claude Code transcript viewers on GitHub, each with a different focus:

- **cc_transcript_viewer (tim-hua-01):** A zero-dependency local web app. It also covers Codex, Cursor, and opencode, and it refreshes live so you can follow an active session. It can also export a session as a standalone HTML file. (git clone https://github.com/tim-hua-01/cc_transcript_viewer.git)
- **Claudescope (vladar107):** A local viewer and search tool that also handles six other agents. It offers full-text search, tool-call views, token and cost analytics, and Markdown export. It is MIT licensed. (It reads Claude Code session transcripts and makes them browsable, searchable, and comparable against other agents' sessions.) The repo is at https://github.com/vladar107/claudescope.
- **claude-code-viewer (esc5221):** A desktop app that renders transcripts with Markdown and syntax highlighting. It is MIT licensed and built with Node.js. (npm run dist:mac is one of its build commands.)
- **claude-code-transcripts (simonw, also a fork by ricklupton):** A Python CLI that turns sessions into paginated HTML pages, with an option to publish to a GitHub Gist. (It converts Claude Code session files (JSON or JSONL) into mobile-friendly HTML pages with pagination.)
- **claude-transcript-viewer (varunr89):** A web server with search and infinite scroll. It is MIT licensed and can be run with npx. (It is a web server for browsing and searching Claude Code conversation transcripts with semantic search, infinite scroll, and collapsible cells.)
- **claude-scrollback (alexdej):** A lightweight viewer with a session browser and static HTML generation. It also adds a resume command for each session.
- **claude-reader (vikasgrac):** A terminal pane that tails the live transcript and shows only the prose you need to read, without the tool-call noise.
- **Claude Code Helper (yaiol):** A two-pane viewer that merges sessions from Windows and WSL distributions. Its licensing is not stated in the results.

Source note: the search results do not show star counts, activity levels, or license details for every project, so check each repo before choosing one.

Several open-source tools browse Claude Code's JSONL session history in a browser:

- **Session storage:** Claude Code saves sessions as JSONL files under ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-uuid>.jsonl, one record per line.
- **Browser viewers:** hitmman55/claude-code-chat-viewer is a single HTML file that turns a transcript into a readable feed with filters and a reader mode. withLinda/claude-JSONL-browser is a web tool that converts the logs into Markdown.
- **Timeline features:** qent/jsonl is a web viewer with message cards, tool calls, results, and timeline navigation. jtklinger/claude-session-viewer is a toolkit that adds a conversation timeline and tool-usage statistics.
- **Terminal and CLI options:** raine/claude-history is a companion CLI, and dmora/ch is a Go CLI that handles subagent conversations.
- **Broader tool:** jhlee0409/claude-code-history-viewer is a desktop and web app that covers Claude Code and many other assistants' histories.

**OpenCode session storage**

- **Current format:** Sources disagree on the exact layout. A SKILL.md guide and a txcript format doc both describe a single SQLite database at `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db`, with session, message, and part tables. txcript also notes that `$XDG_DATA_HOME/opencode/opencode.db` takes precedence when that variable is set, and that an `OPENCODE_DB` env var can override it.
- **Legacy format:** txcript's doc mentions a legacy JSON `storage/` tree that was migrated. A Raycast extension still reads from `~/.local/share/opencode/storage` by default, and a codetether module parses per-session JSON files under `storage/session/`. So older installs may still have JSON files.
- **Exports:** The built-in `/export` reportedly writes only the messages loaded in the TUI, so long sessions can be truncated. One community plugin reads the SQLite store directly and writes Markdown, and another writes transcripts to a `convos/` folder on session idle.

**Agent Trace open standard**

- The Agent Trace spec (agent-trace.dev) is a vendor-neutral format for recording which code in a version-controlled repo came from AI versus humans, including the related agent conversations. It is a data spec, version 0.1.0, status RFC, dated January 2026. Cursor's proposal is the origin, per a post by one of its supporters.
- Other "trace" standards are unrelated and could be confused with it. These include TRACE (trace-spec, a signed attestation receipt for agent runs, v0.2 developer preview, under the Linux Foundation), OpenTrace (a runtime tracing spec for agent systems), and OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions.

I did not verify whether OpenCode writes Agent Trace records. I'd need a search on OpenCode and agent-trace together to check that.

The search turned up no coding-agent-specific conventions. The general GenAI agent conventions are the closest match, and the sources disagree on maturity.

- **Status is contested.** Most sources say the conventions are still in Development. One says the repository currently marks the GenAI conventions as Development, and as of August 21, 2026 it has no official release. Another reports the OTel GenAI SIG has stabilized the GenAI Semantic Conventions in June 2026, but it is a secondary blog and the other sources don't corroborate it. Treat the Development status as the better-supported reading.
- **Repository move.** Core v1.42.0 moved the GenAI definitions into the separate semantic-conventions-genai repository.
- **Agent operations.** The agent conventions define operations such as create_agent, invoke_agent, invoke_workflow, plan, and execute_tool. One source says v1.41 split invoke_agent into CLIENT/INTERNAL span kinds.
- **Tool calls and MCP.** MCP has its own Development conventions for client and server spans, W3C Trace Context propagation, transport correlation, tool-aware attributes, and metrics. The agent metrics include gen_ai.agent.name, gen_ai.tool.name, and gen_ai.tool.status, though that source is the less reliable one.
- **Content and evaluation.** Prompt and output capture is Opt-In, and the OpenTelemetry documentation warns that event support is not yet available in every language. For evaluator results, gen_ai.evaluation.result provides a standard carrier for evaluator scores and explanations.

Nothing I found addresses coding agents such as Claude Code specifically. The sources cover general agent and LLM tracing.

**Claudescope** (vladar107/claudescope) is a local, read-only viewer for AI coding-agent transcripts.

- **Supported agents (8):** Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, JetBrains Junie, pi, opencode, GitHub Copilot CLI, Google Antigravity, and xAI Grok CLI. Each source is optional, and sessions are grouped by project with an agent tag.

- **Indexing:** The app re-scans on an interval (default 15 seconds) and incrementally picks up new or changed transcripts without a restart. Unchanged scans are cheap, and `POST /api/reindex` forces one. The page doesn't describe filesystem watching. Ranked full-text search can lag a live session by up to a minute.

- **Storage:** Its own index is a DuckDB database, not SQLite. It reads opencode's SQLite database read-only through Node's built-in `node:sqlite`. Other state includes a pricing file and a settings file, all under `~/.claudescope/`.

- **Features:**
  - Browsing projects and sessions, with token, cost, and PR details
  - A threaded session reader with diffs, subagent runs, and in-session find
  - A "Files changed" tab
  - Markdown export with optional redaction
  - A memory viewer for instruction files and per-project memory
  - An inventory of skills, MCP servers, hooks, and plugins
  - Full-text search across all agents, with an exact-match mode
  - Token and cost analytics by time, project, model, and agent
  - A cross-agent efficiency comparison and a weekly digest
  - An MCP server, a CLI with JSON output, a Claude Code/Codex plugin, and a Raycast extension

  The page doesn't describe a dedicated timeline view. Analytics "over time" and the digest are the closest equivalents.

- **Tech stack:** Node.js 22.13+, TypeScript, DuckDB (`@duckdb/node-api`), Vitest, and npm. It's distributed through npm, Homebrew, and Nix, and it runs a local server on `127.0.0.1`.

- **License:** MIT, © Vladislav Ramazaev.

- **Stars and activity:** 21 stars, 1 fork, 0 watchers, and 263 commits on `main`. The captured page doesn't show release or contributor details.

- **AI/semantic features:** None are described. Search is BM25 full-text, not semantic. Costs are local list-price estimates computed from token counts. The "agent-distilled" memory is read from the agents' own files, not generated by Claudescope.

Plugin hooks sit in the plugin's `hooks/hooks.json` (or a custom path set in the `hooks` field), and they merge with user and project hooks when the plugin is enabled. Plugin hooks are defined in the plugin's hooks/hooks.json file or in a file given by a custom path to the hooks field. When a plugin is enabled, its hooks are merged with user and project hooks.
- **Matchers:** Events like UserPromptSubmit and Stop don't use matchers, so the matcher field can be omitted (For events like UserPromptSubmit, Notification, Stop, and SubagentStop that don't use matchers, you can omit the matcher field).

Third-party pages list UserPromptSubmit as carrying a `user_prompt` field and PostToolUse as carrying `tool_result`. I couldn't confirm these against the official docs, so treat them as unverified.
- **Plugin file format:** The plugin `hooks.json` needs a top-level `hooks` wrapper around the event names, plus an optional `description`. - **Plugin variables:** Use `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` in command paths for portability. `$CLAUDE_ENV_FILE` is available only to SessionStart hooks, for persisting environment variables.

**Claude Code History Viewer** is a desktop app and headless web server for browsing, searching, and analyzing conversation history from AI coding assistants. The README describes it as "100% offline."

**Supported agents and log locations**
The README lists 31 assistants. Examples:
- **Claude Code:** `~/.claude/projects/`
- **Codex CLI:** `~/.codex/sessions/`
- **Gemini CLI:** `~/.gemini/history/`
- **GitHub Copilot:** `~/.copilot/session-state/` and VS Code `workspaceStorage` chat sessions
- **Cursor:** `~/.cursor/`
- **OpenCode:** `~/.local/share/opencode/`
- **Others:** Cline (incl. Roo Code), Kilo Code, Aider, Kimi, Kiro, Goose, Zed, Qwen Code, Pi, Trae, and more

**Formats:** Storage varies by provider. Common formats are JSON/JSONL files and SQLite databases.

**Features**
- Unified viewer across providers, with filtering and cross-tool comparison
- Browsing by project and session
- Global search across all conversations
- Analytics dashboard with token stats, cost breakdown, and provider distribution
- Session Board for multi-session visual analysis (pixel view, attribute brushing, activity timeline)
- Settings manager, message navigator, and a "Recent Edits" view with restore
- Session export (HTML/JSON) from the command line
- Accessibility support (keyboard navigation, screen reader semantics, high contrast, font scaling)
- Five interface languages

**Tech stack:** Rust and Tauri v2 (backend); React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Vite, and i18next (frontend).

**License:** MIT.

**Live updates:** Yes. It watches session files for changes. In server mode, it pushes updates to the browser via Server-Sent Events.

**AI summarization or semantic clustering:** The README doesn't mention either. Its analytics are token and cost statistics, not AI-generated analysis.

**Installation**
- **Desktop:** Download a `.dmg` (macOS), `.exe`/`.zip` (Windows), or `.AppImage` (Linux) from Releases, or use Homebrew (`brew install --cask jhlee0409/tap/claude-code-history-viewer`).
- **Headless server:** Install `cchv-server` via Homebrew or an install script, or download a prebuilt binary. Run `cchv-server --serve`, which listens on port 3727 by default and requires token authentication unless disabled. Docker, Docker Compose, and systemd setups are also documented.
- **From source:** Clone the repo and use `pnpm` or `just`. This requires Node.js 20.19+ (or 22.12+), pnpm, and a Rust toolchain.

**Supported agents and log locations**

- **Claude Code:** session JSONL files under `~/.claude/projects/`.
- **Codex:** rollout JSONL files under `~/.codex/sessions/` and `~/.codex/archived_sessions/`. Thread metadata comes from `~/.codex/state_5.sqlite` when available.
- **Cursor IDE:** conversations in the `cursorDiskKV` table of `state.vscdb` under `~/Library/Application Support/Cursor/User/globalStorage/`. This source is preferred when present.
- **Cursor CLI:** per-session SQLite `store.db` files under `~/.cursor/chats/<md5(cwd)>/<session-uuid>/`, with a `meta.json` beside each. A lossy JSONL export under `~/.cursor/projects/.../agent-transcripts/` is used only when no `store.db` exists.
- **opencode:** a single SQLite database at `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db` (`session`, `message`, and `part` tables). Sessions use the ids `opencode:<sessionID>`.

**Features**

- A single time-sorted sidebar across all sources, with agent, model, directory, and date filters and content search.
- Transcript rendering with Markdown, LaTeX, images, collapsible thinking blocks, and tool-specific formatting, including diffs.
- Sub-agent and guardian linking, a prompt outline, and jump controls.
- Custom session names, stored in a separate viewer-owned file.
- Copying your prompts as Markdown, and saving a session as a self-contained HTML file.
- Fourteen themes.
- Optional Mica companion daemon that captures transcripts and flags truncations, rewrites, and deletions.
- Exporters that convert Cursor and opencode sessions into Codex rollout format.

**Live refresh**

The sidebar rescans about once per second. An open transcript is checked about three times per second and tails in place while keeping scroll position and expanded blocks. Session metadata is cached by file modification time, so each poll only re-reads changed files. For opencode, change detection also watches the write-ahead log.

**Tech stack**

Python 3.9+ with only the standard library on the server, and vanilla JavaScript with no build step on the frontend. The frontend loads marked, DOMPurify, and KaTeX from a CDN, each pinned to a version with an SRI hash. The app binds to loopback by default and includes a Host-header check against DNS rebinding.

**License:** MIT.

**Install**

Clone the repository and run `python3 server.py`, with no `pip install` or build step. The default URL is `http://127.0.0.1:3132/`. Options include `--port`, `--host`, and paths for each source. Binding to `0.0.0.0` for LAN access requires an explicit flag.

**Caveat:** the README calls the project "vibe-coded" and says it depends on current on-disk transcript formats, so parts may break if those formats change.

- **What ACP is:** It's an open standard from Zed Industries, released in August 2025, that lets editors talk to coding agents. It uses JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdin/stdout. Clients are typically editors, and the editor usually launches the agent as a subprocess (stdin/stdout, line-delimited JSON).

- **Session loading:** Session history is handled by `session/load`. session/new creates a fresh session; session/load resumes a prior one. - **Claude Code:** Claude Code isn't native to ACP. One source notes that some popular coding agents (e.g., Claude Code, Codex CLI) predate ACP, so an adapter is needed. Zed ships with Claude Code (via adapter) pre-configured.

The excerpt cuts off partway through the `SessionStart` section, so the full input schemas for `SessionEnd`, `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop`, and `PreCompact` aren't included. The answers below cover what the excerpt does state.

**1. Hook event names (33)**

`Setup`, `SessionStart`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `UserPromptExpansion`, `PreToolUse`, `PermissionRequest`, `PermissionDenied`, `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `PostToolBatch`, `Notification`, `MessageDisplay`, `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop`, `TaskCreated`, `TaskCompleted`, `Stop`, `StopFailure`, `TeammateIdle`, `InstructionsLoaded`, `ConfigChange`, `CwdChanged`, `DirectoryAdded`, `FileChanged`, `WorktreeCreate`, `WorktreeRemove`, `PreCompact`, `PostCompact`, `PreModelSwitch`, `PostModelSwitch`, `Elicitation`, `ElicitationResult`, `SessionEnd`

**2. Common JSON input fields**

These arrive on stdin for command hooks, or as the POST body for HTTP hooks:

- `session_id`: current session identifier
- `prompt_id`: UUID of the prompt being processed (absent until the first input)
- `transcript_path`: path to the conversation JSON
- `cwd`: current working directory
- `scratchpad_dir`: session scratchpad path (v2.1.257+)
- `permission_mode`: `"default"`, `"plan"`, `"acceptEdits"`, `"auto"`, `"dontAsk"`, or `"bypassPermissions"`
- `effort`: object with a `level` field
- `hook_event_name`: the event that fired

`agent_id` and `agent_type` are also included when a hook fires inside a subagent or when the session uses `--agent`.

**3. Subagents: SubagentStart/SubagentStop**

Yes, hooks fire for subagents.

- `SubagentStart` fires when a subagent is spawned. Its matcher is the agent type (for example `general-purpose`, `Explore`, `Plan`, or a custom name).
- `SubagentStop` fires when a subagent finishes. It uses the same matcher values. It also receives `last_assistant_message`, which carries the subagent's final assistant text.
- Hooks from settings, managed policy, and plugins run inside subagents. Tool events such as `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` carry `agent_id` and `agent_type`.
- A `Stop` hook in subagent frontmatter is converted to `SubagentStop`.
- The excerpt doesn't include the full `SubagentStart` or `SubagentStop` input schemas.

**4. SessionEnd**

Yes, it exists. It fires when a session terminates. Its matcher values, which indicate why the session ended, are:

- `clear`
- `resume`
- `logout`
- `prompt_input_exit`
- `other`

`SessionEnd` hooks share a 1.5-second budget by default. A longer per-hook `timeout` raises the budget, up to 60 seconds. The exit code can't block; stderr goes to the user only.

**5. PreCompact / PostCompact**

Yes, both exist. Their matcher values are `manual` and `auto`.

- `PreCompact` runs before compaction. Exit code 2 blocks compaction.
- `PostCompact` runs after compaction completes. It has no decision control and shows stderr to the user only.

**6. Transcript references**

- `transcript_path` is a common field: "Path to conversation JSON." The file is written asynchronously and can lag the in-memory conversation, so it may not include the current turn's latest messages.
- The docs recommend `last_assistant_message` on `Stop` and `SubagentStop` instead of reading the transcript for the final assistant text.
- `agent_transcript_path` doesn't appear in the excerpt. The subagent transcript location may be documented in the truncated portion, but I can't confirm that.

I have enough context now. Here is what I found, where I'd push back, and the questions I need answered before writing a plan.

**What I found**

- **This is BaselHack 2026**, which runs 30 Oct to 1 Nov, so you have roughly a day. The readme is the BaselHack template. That deadline should drive every scope decision below.
- **The viewer space is crowded.** I found over a dozen Claude Code transcript viewers. Three are serious: [Claudescope](https://github.com/vladar107/claudescope) covers 8 agents with DuckDB search, cost analytics and an MCP server plus Claude plugin. [claude-code-history-viewer](https://github.com/jhlee0409/claude-code-history-viewer) covers 31 agents with file watching and SSE live updates. [cc_transcript_viewer](https://github.com/tim-hua-01/cc_transcript_viewer) is zero-dependency with live tail. All are MIT.
- **None of them do** semantic abstraction levels, semantic clustering, a flow graph of the conversation tree, or project-local shareable state. That gap is your pitch. Timeline, search and cost analytics alone will not win.
- **The transcript is a tree, not a list.** Each record links to its parent, rewinds create branches, subagents live in their own JSONL files next to the session, and compaction leaves summary markers. Branches, subagent nesting and compaction boundaries are free abstraction levels you can show without any LLM call.
- **Hooks beat filesystem watching as the event source.** Claude Code exposes 33 hook events, each delivering the session id, transcript path, cwd and agent id. A plugin can ship them. The docs warn the transcript file lags the live conversation, so hooks should trigger reads of the JSONL, not replace it.
- **Open standards exist but none fit cleanly.** Claude Code exports OpenTelemetry logs natively, but prompt content is opt-in and config is read at startup. The OTel GenAI conventions are still in Development status. ACP from Zed can replay a session via session/load, and opencode speaks ACP, but Claude Code needs an adapter. opencode stores sessions in a single SQLite database, a different model entirely.
- **Single-command install is realistic.** Your local CLI supports the plugin install command directly, so the README line can be a marketplace add plus install.

**Where I challenge the idea**

- **Watching all of ~/.claude is wrong for a project tool.** Scope the engine to the current project's session folder. The rest is other projects' private data.
- **Committing `.yolo-twice` to git is a privacy trap.** Transcripts contain pasted secrets and tool output. Store only derived artifacts there, in plain JSON files rather than a binary database so git diffs and merges work, with an explicit export step for sharing.
- **Define idempotency concretely.** Key every derived artifact by the hash of its input records plus the analyzer version. Re-running produces byte-identical files, which is what makes stop and resume trivial.
- **LLM analysis during indexing is the biggest risk** for a day-long hackathon. Branch and compaction structure, tool-call grouping and BM25 search give you three abstraction levels with zero LLM cost. Add LLM summaries only on top, via the headless `claude -p` command so no API key is needed.
- **Build the parser on an existing MIT project** rather than from scratch. Claudescope's Node parser or cc_transcript_viewer's Python one already handle subagents, sidechains and tool results.

**Questions I cannot answer myself**

1. Who is the primary user in the demo: a developer reviewing their own long session, or a team lead reviewing a colleague's?
2. Should `.yolo-twice` ever contain raw transcript copies, or only derived summaries, indexes and annotations?
3. Are LLM calls during indexing acceptable, and if so via subscription through the headless CLI or via an API key?
4. Pitch format: a Markdown deck rendered on the same GitHub Pages site, or a PowerPoint from the corporate template?
5. What does the name "yolo-twice" mean, and are there branding constraints?
6. Do you want me to propose the four-person module split, or do you already have one?

The four decisions below change the plan most, so I'd like them answered first.

{"command":"mkdir -p ~/.claude/plans && cat > $PROJECT/documentation/design.md <<'EOF' # yolo-twice: design and hackathon plan Status: draft, 31 Oct 2026, decided together in the kickoff Q&A. Edit freely. ## 1. Context Long Claude Code sessions are black boxes: a single session JSONL grows to megabytes, spawns subagent transcripts, branches on rewind and gets compacted. Existing viewers render this as a flat chat list. yolo-twice makes a running session navigable at several levels of abstraction, live, and stores what it learns next to the project so it can be committed or ignored. Built at BaselHack 2026 (30 Oct to 1 Nov) by four people working AI-driven in parallel. Demo on 1 Nov is a vertical slice; the architecture is designed for the full vision. ### Decisions taken | Topic | Decision | |---|---| | Deadline | Demo slice on 1 Nov, continue afterwards | | Pitch features | Semantic zoom, live flow graph, shareable project history. Cross-agent later | | Event source | Claude Code hooks trigger ingestion; the session JSONL is the source of truth; file watcher as fallback | | Stack | Node/TypeScript monorepo (pnpm workspaces) | | Primary user | Developer reviewing their own sessions; team sharing is a later layer on the same data | | `.yolo-twice` content | Redacted raw events plus derived data, so it is safe to commit | | LLM analysis | Headless `claude -p` through the user's subscription, hash-cached, never blocking the UI | | Pitch | Markdown deck on GitHub Pages, reusing the site's mermaid diagrams | ### What exists and what we add Over a dozen Claude Code transcript viewers exist. The strongest are [Claudescope](https://github.com/vladar107/claudescope) (8 agents, DuckDB search, MCP server, plugin), [claude-code-history-viewer](https://github.com/jhlee0409/claude-code-history-viewer) (31 agents, file watch, SSE) and [cc_transcript_viewer](https://github.com/tim-hua-01/cc_transcript_viewer) (zero dependencies, live tail). None of them offer abstraction levels, a conversation flow graph, or project-local committable state. We reuse their parsing knowledge and build the three missing things. ## 2. Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR CC[Claude Code session] -- "hooks (HTTP POST)" --> ENG CC -- writes --> JSONL[(~/.claude/projects/<slug>/*.jsonl
+ subagents/*.jsonl)] JSONL -- "incremental read from cursor" --> ENG[Engine daemon] WATCH[File watcher fallback] --> ENG ENG --> NORM[Normalize + redact] NORM --> STORE[(.yolo-twice/
events.ndjson, structure.json, semantic/)] STORE --> AN[Analyzers
structural, search, semantic via claude -p] AN --> STORE ENG -- "HTTP + SSE" --> UI[Web UI
zoom, flow graph, timeline, search] PLUGIN[Claude plugin
/yolo-twice, /yolo-twice stop] --> ENG ``` ### Packages (monorepo under `code/`) | Package | Responsibility | Owner | |---|---|---| | `packages/core` | Event schema, source adapters (claude-code now, opencode later), redaction, cursor-based incremental reader, `.yolo-twice` store | A | | `packages/engine` | Daemon: HTTP API, SSE stream, `/hook` endpoint, watcher fallback, analyzer queue, pid/port lifecycle, CLI (`yolo-twice start|stop|status|index`) | A | | `packages/analyzers` | Structural tree (L0 to L4), full-text search, semantic phase summaries and cluster labels via `claude -p`, cost rollups | B | | `packages/ui` | Vite + React web app: zoom view (stretchtext), flow graph, timeline, search, live updates over SSE | C | | `plugin/` | Claude Code plugin: `plugin.json`, `commands/yolo-twice.md`, `hooks/hooks.json`, `bin/yolo-twice` | D | | `site/` and `assets/pitch/` | VitePress site and Slidev deck, both with native mermaid, deployed to GitHub Pages by one Actions workflow | D | | `fixtures/` | Two or three real sessions, redacted, so B and C can develop without the engine running | D | ## 3. Live pipeline ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant CC as Claude Code participant H as hook (HTTP) participant E as Engine participant S as .yolo-twice participant UI as Web UI CC->>H: UserPromptSubmit / PostToolUse / SubagentStop / PostCompact / Stop H->>E: POST /hook {session_id, transcript_path, agent_id, hook_event_name} E->>E: debounce 300 ms per transcript E->>S: read new lines from cursor, normalize, redact, append events.ndjson E->>S: update structure.json (structural levels, no LLM) E-->>UI: SSE: events, structure E->>E: enqueue semantic jobs for changed phases (hash-keyed) E->>S: write semantic/.json when claude -p returns E-->>UI: SSE: semantic ``` The transcript file lags the live conversation, so every hook triggers a re-read from the cursor and the next hook or watcher event picks up anything missed. Hooks of type `http` post straight to the engine; if the engine is not running the hook fails silently and the watcher catches up when `/yolo-twice` starts it. ## 4. Data model ### Normalized event (one JSON line in `events.ndjson`) Field names follow OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions where they exist (`gen_ai.*` equivalents noted in the schema file). ```json { "id": "record uuid, or sha256 of the line for records without one", "ts": "2026-10-31T08:12:03.702Z", "session": "34b27ceb-...", "agent": "claude-code", "agent_id": null, "parent": "parentUuid or null", "kind": "user.prompt | assistant.text | assistant.thinking | tool.call | tool.result | subagent.start | subagent.stop | compaction | cost | title | system | meta", "tool": { "name": "Bash", "call_id": "toolu_..." }, "text": "redacted content", "model": "claude-fable-5-1", "usage": { "input_tokens": 0, "output_tokens": 0, "cache_read_tokens": 0 }, "redacted": { "count": 2, "rules": ["api-key", "env-value"] }, "src": { "file": "relative path under ~/.claude", "line": 123 } } ``` Mapping from [... truncated 6337 chars, sha256 45a706bd8575f536 ...] g, embedding-based clustering, OpenTelemetry export, standalone binary. ## 9. Site and pitch The README carries the mermaid diagrams and renders them on GitHub as-is. The VitePress site reuses the README sections. The Slidev deck lives in `assets/pitch/`, renders the same mermaid sources, exports to PDF and deploys under `/pitch` on the same Pages site. Pitch arc, three minutes: a multi-megabyte session JSONL on screen as the problem; one sentence on why existing viewers do not solve it; live demo zooming out to phases, in to a tool call, and the flow graph showing a rewind branch and subagents; the architecture diagram; the one-line install; roadmap. ## 10. consider tradeof near realtime updates ( costly in CPU and tokens) vs low frequency. Can we give the user the choice, ie slider "micro management" <---> "yolo"

Good question, and it exposes something the design glossed over: not all layers cost the same, so the slider should not throttle everything uniformly.

**Where the cost actually sits**

| Layer | Cost per event | Realtime safe? |
|---|---|---|
| Ingest, normalize, redact, append | microseconds, linear in new bytes | yes, always |
| Structural tree and search index | milliseconds, incremental | yes |
| Flow graph re-layout in the browser | noticeable with thousands of nodes | throttle |
| Semantic summaries via `claude -p` | seconds to minutes, thousands of tokens, one Node process spawn | no |
| Pushing updates at the user | attention, not CPU | this is the real "micro management" |

The expensive layer is semantic work, and it has a trap: re-summarizing an open phase after every turn is quadratic in tokens over the phase, and every interim result is a cache miss by design because the input hash keeps changing. It also competes with your own Claude Code session for the same subscription rate limit, which is a strong argument against eager summarization as the default.

**So yes, give the choice, but make the slider control triggers and attention, not ingestion**

Ingestion always runs near realtime because it is nearly free. That way the data is always complete and zooming in is instant regardless of mode. The slider decides when semantic work is triggered and how much the UI pushes at you. I'd use a slider with four detents rather than a continuous value, since the modes are qualitatively different and need testing:

| Detent | Semantic trigger | Default zoom | UI behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| Micro management | every turn, incremental fold summary of the open phase with a small model | L3 steps | live ticker, graph re-layout batched to 1 s |
| Attentive | turn label on each Stop hook, phase summary when a phase closes | L2 turns | live, no interim phase summaries |
| Balanced (default) | phase close only: compaction, idle gap, topic change | L1 phases | updates on phase boundaries |
| Yolo | nothing automatic; summaries computed lazily when the UI shows the node, or on SessionEnd | L0 digest | "catch me up" button summarizes everything since you last looked |

Two details make this clean:

- **Viewport is the demand signal.** The UI requests summaries for visible nodes. Yolo is pure lazy, micro is eager prefetch of everything. Same code path, different prefetch policy.
- **Idempotency survives the slider.** A closed phase has the same input hash in every mode, so the artifact is identical whether it was computed eagerly or lazily. Interim summaries of open phases are marked `interim` and written to the gitignored cache, never to the committed sessions folder. Switching modes never produces conflicting committed files.

The "catch me up" digest is the strongest feature of yolo mode and fits the pitch: you let the agent run, go for coffee, and come back to a summary of what happened since your last look, from the engine's last-viewed cursor.

Show the cost next to the slider: an estimated tokens-per-hour and update lag readout, so the tradeoff is explicit rather than hidden. The setting lives in the project config with a per-user override, is changeable live from the UI header or `/yolo-twice mode yolo`, and the engine reloads it without restart.

import { render } from 'pele';

const { svg } = render(`flowchart LR
  A[Mermaid text] --> B[SVG]`);

document.querySelector('#diagram').innerHTML = svg;
```

claude-code-transcripts is a Python tool that converts Claude Code session files (JSON or JSONL) into multi-page HTML transcripts that are readable on mobile. It can read local sessions from `~/.claude/projects`, import a session by file path or URL, or convert all local sessions into a browsable archive with per-project pages. Each transcript has an `index.html` with a timeline of prompts and commits, plus paginated `page-001.html`-style transcript pages. Notable design choices include pagination, optional upload to a GitHub Gist (requiring the `gh` CLI) with a gisthost.github.io preview link that the tool patches to fix relative links, and an option to bundle the original session file. The README warns that the `web` commands are currently broken because of changes to unofficial APIs, and the page doesn't mention any redaction of sensitive content. The project is licensed under Apache-2.0 and has about 1.7k stars.

ccusage is a command-line tool that analyzes token usage and costs for coding agent CLIs. Its repository describes it as a way to "Analyze coding (agent) CLI token usage and costs from local data." It reads the usage records that tools such as Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Gemini CLI keep on the local machine, then summarizes them by day, week, month, or session, with token and cache counts, USD cost estimates, per-model breakdowns, and optional JSON output. Pricing relies on a LiteLLM pricing file, and an offline mode can use cached pricing data. The project is released under the MIT License, with copyright held by ryoppippi. It appears actively maintained: it has about 2,880 commits, roughly 19.3k stars, and a scheduled workflow that refreshes pricing data and opens pull requests. The page doesn't show the date of the latest commit, so I can't confirm how recent the most recent changes are.

**Install:** Install from npm, or load it from a jsDelivr CDN script tag. The CDN build exposes a global `pele` object with a `mount()` function.

**API:**
- `render(text)` is synchronous. It returns an object with an `svg` string that you insert into the page yourself.
- `mount(element, text)` is browser-only. It renders into an element, reads fonts from CSS, and adapts the layout to the container width.
- `renderAsync(text)` from `pele/lazy` is awaited and loads diagram types on demand.
- Smaller bundles are possible by importing `register()` from `pele/core` and registering only the diagram types you need, such as `pele/diagrams/flowchart`.
- The README doesn't cover options or error handling. It points to pele.run/api for those.

**CSS theming:** Set these variables on `.pele` or a parent element:
- Colors: `--pele-bg`, `--pele-fg`, `--pele-muted`, `--pele-line`, `--pele-surface`, `--pele-surface-alt`, `--pele-border`, `--pele-accent`
- Font and shape: `--pele-font`, `--pele-radius`
- Chart series: `--pele-series-1` through `--pele-series-8`

Theme changes apply without re-rendering the diagram.

**Diagram types:** It supports the full set of diagram types included in Mermaid 12.1.0.

**Bundle formats:** It ships as ES modules for npm use, with subpath imports, and as a global browser build (`pele.global.js`) for CDN use.

**License:** MIT. The Mermaid-derived specs under `tests/compat` and their grammar files are also MIT-licensed.

**Limitations:** The README doesn't list unsupported Mermaid features. It says Pele "targets Mermaid 12.1.0 syntax, with its own layout and visual style," so output will look different from Mermaid's. For security, it escapes diagram text, filters links and styles, and limits source and output size. Handling untrusted input, displaying errors, and supplying icons are covered on the security page.

**Node (SSR) vs. browser:** The README doesn't state this directly. `render()` is synchronous, has no runtime dependencies, and returns a string, so it likely works on a server. `mount()` needs a DOM, so it's browser-only. This is my inference from the API, so verify it before relying on it.

new='''### Semantic zoom: two axes

Zoom is not a fixed ladder of five levels. It has two independent axes, and both apply at every
node, including the top.

**Structural axis** (what unit is shown):

| Level | Unit | Source | LLM needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| L-1 | Project: all sessions of this project | session list | no (digest: yes) |
| L0 | Session: title, duration, cost, outcome | title and cost records | no |
| L1 | Phases: "setting up auth", "debugging tests" | semantic analyzer; structural fallback splits on compaction, long gaps and topic-changing prompts | yes (fallback no) |
| L2 | Turns: user prompt to final assistant text, subagent runs collapsed into one node | parent chain | no |
| L3 | Steps: tool calls with results, thinking, subagent internals | content blocks | no |
| L4 | Raw record | JSONL line | no |

**Text axis** (how much text a node shows), in the stretchtext sense: any text can be
collapsed in place to a shorter form and expanded back.

| Granularity | Target | Example at L0 |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | one line | "Migrated auth to OIDC, tests green" |
| `abstract` | up to three sentences | what, why, outcome |
| `summary` | a paragraph or short list | the phases and the decisions in each |
| `full` | the complete text | all turns |

The two axes combine: zooming out at the top collapses the session summary to a title, and
one step further shows the project as a list of session titles, which can itself be
summarized into a project digest. Zooming in on a long tool result or a long assistant
message collapses it to an abstract first, then expands to full text. A long paragraph is
therefore never the end of the road: it can always be zoomed out one more step.

Every (node, granularity) pair is a derived artifact under
`sessions/<id>/text/<node-id>.<granularity>.<hash>.json`, keyed by the hash of the node's
input text plus the analyzer version, produced lazily (see the attention slider) or by a
structural fallback (head and tail plus counts) when no LLM result exists yet. Shorter
granularities are built from the next longer one, so the cost is a fold, not a re-read.

Each structure node has `id`, `level`, `children`, `span` (first and last event id) and the
available granularities. The UI expands any node in place, so the user can read the whole
session at one granularity and dive where needed.

### Flow graph

The engine emits the graph as mermaid text in `sessions/<id>/graph.mmd`, one file per
structural level requested. Nodes are L2 turns by default, expandable to L3. Edges: `parent`
(sequence), `tool.call` to `tool.result`, `subagent.start` to its transcript, and branch
edges where one parent has several children (a rewind). Zooming out merges turns into phase
nodes, like map tiles. The UI renders the text with [pele](https://pele.run/) (MIT, from the
Obsidian team), the same renderer the site and the deck use, and attaches click handlers to
the SVG node ids to zoom. Mermaid text is readable, diffable and committable, and renders on
GitHub as-is. If interactivity outgrows SVG, `@xyflow/react` is the fallback.

'''

The page covers this under Claude Code skills. Custom commands (`.claude/commands/*.md`) were merged into skills and work the same way, so the rules below apply to both.

## Inline shell execution (`` !`command` ``)

Claude Code runs the command before the content is sent to Claude, and the output replaces the placeholder:

```markdown
## Current changes

!`git diff HEAD`
```

- The inline form is recognized only when `!` is at the start of a line or follows whitespace. In `KEY=!`cmd``, it stays literal and doesn't run.
- For multi-line commands, use a fenced block opened with ` ```! `:

  ````markdown
  ```!
  node --version
  git status --short
  ```
  ````
- A non-zero exit code aborts the whole invocation, and Claude never sees the content. Exit code 1 from search and comparison commands is the exception. To tolerate other failures, append `|| true`.
- Output is inserted as plain text and isn't re-scanned for more `!` placeholders.

## Frontmatter and `allowed-tools`

`allowed-tools` pre-approves tools for the turn that invokes the command. It accepts a space- or comma-separated string or a YAML list:

```yaml
---
description: Stage and commit the current changes
disable-model-invocation: true
allowed-tools: Bash(git add *) Bash(git commit *) Bash(git status *)
---
```

- `Bash(git add *)` allows `git add` with any arguments. `Bash(name)` without a `*` matches the exact command.
- Injected commands are checked against your permission rules and don't prompt. A command that isn't allowed, including one a rule would normally ask about, aborts the invocation. Pre-approve it here to avoid that. Deny rules still override `allowed-tools`.
- The grant lasts until your next message.
- Commands in `.claude/commands/` accept the same frontmatter fields except `name` and `paths`.

## Arguments

- `$ARGUMENTS`: the full argument string as typed.
- `$ARGUMENTS[N]` or `$N`: a 0-based positional argument. Quote multi-word values, as in `/my-skill "hello world" second`.
- `$name`: a named argument declared with `arguments: [issue, branch]` in the frontmatter, mapped by position.
- If no placeholder receives the arguments, Claude Code appends `ARGUMENTS: <value>` to the content.
- Escape a literal dollar sign with a backslash, as in `\$1.00`.

```markdown
---
description: Fix a GitHub issue
---
Fix GitHub issue $ARGUMENTS. Branch name: $1
```

## Namespacing for plugin commands

The page's naming table gives the pattern for plugin skills as `/plugin-name:skill-name`. For a plugin named `yolo-twice` with a skill at `skills/yolo-twice/SKILL.md`, the command is **`/yolo-twice:yolo-twice`**. The bare `/yolo-twice` isn't listed as a valid form for this layout.

If the plugin's `SKILL.md` sits at the plugin root, the command is named from its `name` field, falling back to the plugin directory name.

## `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`

# Plugin manifest reference

> Complete reference for plugin.json: every field with its type and default, accepted path forms, and the userConfig and environment variable schemas.

A plugin manifest is the `plugin.json` file in a plugin's `.claude-plugin/` directory. It carries the plugin's metadata and the [`userConfig`](#user-configuration) values that Claude Code prompts the user for. It also declares any component that you define inline or keep outside its [default location](#standard-layout).

This reference is for plugin creators, and for marketplace owners who put component fields in a marketplace entry.

> [!NOTE]
>
> These cases are covered on other pages:
>
> * **Learning to build a plugin**: start with [Create a plugin](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/create.md)
> * **What each component does at runtime**: see [Plugin components](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/components.md)

Start at the section that matches what you're looking up:

* A field: the [Fields table](#fields) gives each field's type, whether it's required, its default, and what it accepts. [Path rules](#path-rules) covers the `./` prefix and containment for every component path
* A `userConfig` option or a `channels` entry: the [User configuration](#user-configuration) and [Channels](#channels) schemas
* `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` or another variable a plugin can reference: [Environment variables](#environment-variables)
* Where each component's files go: [Standard layout](#standard-layout)
* A message from `claude plugin validate`: the [troubleshooting page](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/troubleshooting.md) lists each message with its fix and links to the relevant sections on this page

## Manifest file

The manifest is optional. Without it, Claude Code loads the components it finds in the [standard layout](#standard-layout). The plugin name then comes from the marketplace entry, or from the directory name when you load the plugin with `--plugin-dir`.

Write a manifest when you want metadata, a component outside its default directory, `userConfig`, or an inline component definition.

Save the manifest at `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` under the plugin root. Put every other plugin file at the plugin root, not inside `.claude-plugin/`. That includes `skills/`, `commands/`, and `hooks/`.

The following example sets most of the keys in the [Fields table](#fields). It passes validation in a plugin directory that contains each referenced path.

```json theme={null}
{
  "name": "deploy-tools",
  "displayName": "Deploy Tools",
  "version": "1.2.0",
  "description": "Deployment commands, a review agent, and a status monitor",
  "author": {
    "name": "Example Team",
    "email": "dev@example.com",
    "url": "https://example.com"
  },
  "homepage": "https://example.com/docs/deploy-tools",
  "repository": "https://github.com/example/deploy-tools",
  "license": "MIT",
  "keywords": ["deployment", "ci"],
  "defaultEnabled": true,
  "dependencies": ["secrets-vault"],
  "metadata": { "catalogId": "cat-123" },
  "skills": ["./extra-skills/"],
  "commands": {
    "status": {
      "source": "./commands/status.md",
      "description": "Show the current deployment status"
    },
    "about": {
      "content": "Explain what the deploy-tools plugin provides.",
      "description": "Describe this plugin"
    }
  },
  "agents": ["./agents/reviewer.md"],
  "hooks": "./config/extra-hooks.json",
  "mcpServers": {
    "deploy-api": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/server.js"]
    }
  },
  "lspServers": "./.lsp.json",
  "outputStyles": "./styles/",
  "experimental": {
    "themes": "./themes/",
    "monitors": "./config/monitors.json"
  },
  "userConfig": {
    "api_token": {
      "type": "string",
      "title": "API token",
      "description": "Token for the deployment API",
      "sensitive": true
    }
  }
}
```

### Unrecognized fields

An unrecognized top-level key is stripped, and an unrecognized key inside a `userConfig` option, `channels` entry, `lspServers` config, or `monitors` entry is rejected:

* **Top-level fields**: the field is stripped and the plugin loads. `claude plugin validate` reports each unrecognized top-level field as a warning
* **Strict objects**: `userConfig` options, `channels` entries, `lspServers` configs, and `monitors` entries are strict. An unknown key inside one is an error, and the plugin doesn't load

### Validate the manifest

`claude plugin validate` is the authoritative check for a manifest. Run it from your shell against the plugin directory:

```bash theme={null}
claude plugin validate ./my-plugin
```

The command reports one of these results:

* **`Validation passed`**: the manifest loads
* **`Validation passed with warnings`**: the manifest loads, but the validator found something to fix, such as an unknown top-level field that Claude Code strips, a `name` that isn't kebab-case, or a missing `version`, `description`, or `author`. Pass `--strict` to turn warnings into failures in CI
* **`Validation failed`**: the manifest has a type mismatch, a path that is missing or escapes the plugin root, or an unknown key inside a `userConfig` option, `channels` entry, `lspServers` config, or `monitors` entry. Claude Code reports the same problem when it loads the plugin

The command also checks each MCP server entry the plugin declares in `.mcp.json`, in a `.json` file that [`mcpServers`](#mcpservers) names, or inline in `plugin.json`. These MCP checks require Claude Code v2.1.281 or later and include:

* **Errors**: an entry Claude Code would drop when it loads the plugin, a `${user_config.KEY}` reference to an option the manifest doesn't declare, and a remote `url` that isn't a valid absolute URL
* **Warnings**: an `http://` or `ws://` URL to a non-loopback host, and 
[... truncated 35146 chars, sha256 21cef9d6e2e06350 ...]
s for that same event, and events only the manifest declares keep theirs
* **`plugin.json` present, `strict: false`**: an entry that declares any of `commands`, `agents`, `skills`, `hooks`, `outputStyles`, or `themes` is a conflict, and the plugin fails to load with `Plugin <name> has conflicting manifests`

When a [marketplace entry whose `source` is the marketplace root](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/marketplace-reference) lists specific `skills` subdirectories, only those subdirectories load, and the plugin's default `skills/` directory isn't scanned. A `skills` key in the manifest instead [adds to the default](#how-each-key-combines-with-its-default-location).

### Metadata precedence

Some metadata fields have a fixed precedence regardless of `strict`:

* **`defaultEnabled` and display fields**: the entry's `defaultEnabled` and its [display fields](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/marketplace-reference.md#entry-and-plugin-json) such as `displayName` override the manifest's
* **`version`**: the manifest's `version` overrides the entry's
* **`name`**: when the entry lists the plugin under a different `name` than the manifest, `enabledPlugins` uses the entry name, and components are namespaced under the manifest name

For the full precedence table, see [Strict mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/marketplace-reference.md).

# Marketplace reference

> Complete reference for marketplace.json fields, plugin entries, and the plugin and marketplace source objects, with where each is valid.

`marketplace.json` is the file that defines a plugin marketplace. It contains the marketplace's name, its owner, and one entry per plugin. Each entry's plugin source says where Claude Code fetches that plugin from.

A marketplace source is a separate object that says where Claude Code fetches the marketplace file itself. You write one in settings, or Claude Code builds one when you run `claude plugin marketplace add`.

This reference is for marketplace maintainers who need an exact field name or value, and for administrators who need to know which `source` values are valid in [`extraKnownMarketplaces`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#extraknownmarketplaces), [`strictKnownMarketplaces`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#strictknownmarketplaces), and [`blockedMarketplaces`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/org#restrict-what-users-can-install).

> [!NOTE]
>
> These cases are covered on other pages:
>
> * **Building or hosting a marketplace**: see [Create a marketplace](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/create-marketplace.md) and [Host and maintain a marketplace](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/host-marketplace.md)
> * **Allowlist and blocklist recipes**: see [Manage plugins for your organization](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/org.md)

Find the section for what you're writing or reading:

* **The marketplace file**: [Top-level fields](#top-level-fields) and [Plugin entries](#plugin-entries)
* **An entry's `source`**: [Plugin sources](#plugin-sources)
* **A `source` object in settings**: [Marketplace sources](#marketplace-sources)
* **Output from [`claude plugin validate <path>`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/cli-reference)**: [Validation messages](#validation-messages), which maps each message to the field it names

## Marketplace file

Save the marketplace file at `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` in your marketplace's directory. If you keep the file somewhere else in the repository, users have to declare the marketplace in [`extraKnownMarketplaces`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#extraknownmarketplaces) with `path` set on its source, because `claude plugin marketplace add` has no option for it.

The directory that contains `.claude-plugin/` is called the marketplace root, and every relative plugin source resolves from it, not from `.claude-plugin/`.

Each user registers one marketplace per `name`, so a user can't have two marketplaces with the same name registered at once.

Claude Code ignores an unknown top-level key or plugin-entry key rather than rejecting it, so a typo loads silently. `claude plugin validate` reports each unknown key as a warning.

### Reserved names

You can't give your marketplace any of the following names:

* **Official marketplace names**: `claude-code-marketplace`, `claude-code-plugins`, `claude-plugins-official`, `anthropic-marketplace`, `anthropic-plugins`, `agent-skills`, `anthropic-agent-skills`, `life-sciences`, `knowledge-work-plugins`, `claude-for-legal`, `claude-for-financial-services`, `financial-services-plugins`, `first-party-plugins`, and `claude-tag-plugins`. Reserved unless the marketplace comes from a `github` or `git` [marketplace source](#marketplace-sources) under `github.com/anthropics/`.
* **Community marketplace names**: `claude-community`, `claude-plugins-community`, and `healthcare`. Reserved under the same rule as the official names.
* **Plugin directory names**: `anthropic-plugin-directory` and `claude-plugin-directory`. Reserved under the same rule as the official names.
* **Names that impersonate an official marketplace**: names such as `official-claude-plugins` or `claude-plugins-v2`, and any name containing a non-ASCII character. The error is `Marketplace name impersonates an official Anthropic/Claude marketplace`. A control or bidirectional-formatting character in a name also reports `Marketplace name cannot contain control or bidirectional-formatting characters`. A marketplace already registered under such a name stops loading, along with its plugins.
* **Another spelling of a reserved name**: a name that differs from a reserved name only by a trailing dot, or by a symbol other than an underscore in place of a hyphen, so `claude.code.plugins` counts as `claude-code-plugins`. Adding the marketplace fails with [`is another spelling of "<reserved>", a reserved marketplace name`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/errors#marketplace-name-is-another-spelling-of-a-reserved-name), and a marketplace already registered under one stops loading. This check requires Claude Code v2.1.280 or later.
* **Names Claude Code uses for plugins that don't come from a marketplace**: `inline` for plugins loaded with [`--plugin-dir`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference), `builtin` for built-in plugins, `skills-dir` for plugins auto-loaded from [`.claude/skills/`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills), and `synced` for plugins synced from your claude.ai account. `claude-plugin-test` is also reserved. `skills-dir` also appears as `{"source": "skills-dir"}` in `strictKnownMarketplaces` and `blockedMarketplaces`, described under [Source values valid only in policy lists](#source-values-valid-only-in-policy-lists).
* **`npm`, `pip`, `uv`, `cargo`, `github`, and `gh`**: reserved in any casing. This check requires Claude Code v2.1.275 or later.
* **Member names that every JavaScript object has**: `constructor`, `hasOwnProperty`, `isPrototypeOf`, `propertyIsEnumerable`, `toLocaleString`, `toString`, and `valueOf`. `claude plugin marketplace add` refuses a marketplace that uses one with [`Claude Code reserves this name a
[... truncated 40325 chars, sha256 d12e30d89e2b1e01 ...]
 |
| `Plugin name "x" is not accepted by Claude Desktop (letters, digits, ".", "_", "-"; must start alphanumeric; max 128 chars)` | Warning | `plugins[i].name`. Claude Desktop drops the entry |

### Invalid input on a source

`Invalid input` on a `source` means the object matched no source type. Check for these causes:

* An `npm` `package` containing `..`
* A `source` type that isn't one of the [plugin sources](#plugin-sources)
* A known type with a required field missing or of the wrong type, such as `github` without `repo`

A relative path that doesn't start with `./`, other than `"."` or a [bare name under `metadata.pluginRoot`](#relative-path-plugin-source), fails with `Invalid string: must start with "./"`. Before v2.1.285, it printed `Invalid input` like the causes above.

### Failures that validation doesn't catch

`claude plugin validate` doesn't report every failure. An entry `hooks` written as a file path or array passes validation, and the error appears only when the plugin loads, as [Hooks in an entry](#hooks-in-an-entry) describes. Errors fetching a `source` also appear only after install, not in validation.

[`claude plugin list`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/cli-reference) shows a plugin that failed to load with its error, and [Troubleshoot plugins](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/troubleshooting.md) covers the load-time strings.

### Stop

Runs when the main Claude Code agent has finished responding. Does not run if
the stoppage occurred due to a user interrupt. API errors fire
[StopFailure](#stopfailure) instead.

> [!TIP]
>
> The [`/goal`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/goal) command is a built-in shortcut for a session-scoped prompt-based Stop hook. Use it when you want Claude to keep working toward a condition without writing hook configuration.

#### Stop input

In addition to the [common input fields](#common-input-fields), Stop hooks receive `stop_hook_active`, `last_assistant_message`, `background_tasks`, and `session_crons`. The `stop_hook_active` field is `true` when Claude Code is already continuing as a result of a stop hook. Check this value or process the transcript to avoid blocking on a condition that will never resolve.

Claude Code applies an 8-consecutive-continuation cap: after stop hooks have continued the turn eight times in a row, Claude Code overrides the next block and ends the turn. The count of consecutive continuations resets each time Claude calls a tool. To raise the cap, set [`CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars).

The `last_assistant_message` field contains the text content of Claude's final response, so hooks can access it without parsing the transcript file. For hooks that act on the just-completed turn, such as read-aloud or notification hooks, use this field rather than reading `transcript_path`: the transcript file isn't guaranteed to include the final message at Stop time on all versions.

The `background_tasks` and `session_crons` arrays let hooks distinguish "session is done" from "session is paused waiting for background work to wake it back up". Both arrays are present when the task registry is reachable and are empty when nothing is in flight or scheduled.

Each entry in `background_tasks` describes one in-flight task and uses these fields:

| Field | Description |
### PostCompact

Runs after Claude Code completes a compact operation. Use this event to react to the new compacted state, for example to log the generated summary or update external state. Claude Code discards a PostCompact hook's `systemMessage` and `continue` fields.

The same matcher values apply as for `PreCompact`:

| Matcher | When it fires |
| :- | :- |
| `manual` | After `/compact` |
| `auto` | After auto-compact when the conversation reaches the [auto-compact window](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#set-the-auto-compact-window), and after [idle compaction](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md#idlecompaction) |

#### PostCompact input

In addition to the [common input fields](#common-input-fields), PostCompact hooks receive `trigger` and `compact_summary`. The `compact_summary` field contains the conversation summary generated by the compact operation.

```json theme={null}
{
  "session_id": "abc123",
  "transcript_path": "~/.claude/projects/.../00893aaf-19fa-41d2-8238-13269b9b3ca0.jsonl",
  "cwd": "~",
  "hook_event_name": "PostCompact",
  "trigger": "manual",
  "compact_summary": "Summary of the compacted conversation..."
}
```

PostCompact hooks have no decision control. They can't affect the compaction result but can perform follow-up tasks.

### PreModelSwitch

Runs before Claude Code applies a model switch that you or a client requested. Use it to block a switch, require confirmation, or show what the switch will cost before it happens.

PreModelSwitch requires Claude Code v2.1.251 or later. Claude Code runs it for these requests:
### SessionEnd

Runs when a Claude Code session ends. Useful for cleanup tasks, logging session
statistics, or saving session state. Supports matchers to filter by exit reason.

The `reason` field in the hook input indicates why the session ended:

| Reason | Description |
| :- | :- |
| `clear` | Session cleared with `/clear` command |
| `resume` | Session switched via interactive `/resume` |
| `logout` | User logged out |
| `prompt_input_exit` | User exited while prompt input was visible |
| `other` | Other exit reasons |
| `bypass_permissions_disabled` | Removed in v2.1.234; Claude Code doesn't send it. Drop it from your `SessionEnd` matchers |

#### SessionEnd input

In addition to the [common input fields](#common-input-fields), SessionEnd hooks receive a `reason` field indicating why the session ended. See the [reason table](#sessionend) above for all values.

```json theme={null}
{
  "session_id": "abc123",
  "transcript_path": "~/.claude/projects/.../00893aaf-19fa-41d2-8238-13269b9b3ca0.jsonl",
  "cwd": "~",
  "hook_event_name": "SessionEnd",
  "reason": "other"
}
```

SessionEnd hooks have no decision control. They can't block session termination but can perform cleanup tasks. Claude Code discards their [JSON output fields](#json-output), such as `systemMessage`.

SessionEnd hooks have a default timeout of 1.5 seconds. It applies when you exit, run `/clear`, or switch sessions with interactive `/resume`. You can give a hook more time in two ways:

* **Per-hook `timeout`**: set `timeout` in that hook's configuration. The overall budget rises automatically to match the highest per-hook `timeout` in your settings files, up to 60 seconds. If you raise the budget this way, a hook without its own `timeout` still keeps the default. Timeouts set on plugin-provided hooks don't raise the budget.
* **`CLAUDE_CODE_SESSIONEND_HOOKS_TIMEOUT_MS`**: set this environment variable in milliseconds to override the budget explicitly. The value you set also becomes the timeout for each hook without its own `timeout`.

{"url":"https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks","prompt":"Find the configuration section describing hook handler types, specifically HTTP hooks (type \"http\"). Quote the exact JSON for an http hook handler entry (fields: type, url, headers, timeout, allowedEnvVars, onFailure, statusMessage...), what is sent in the POST body (is it the same JSON as the stdin for command hooks?), what response is expected (can it be empty / 200 with no body?), and how connection errors or non-2xx responses are handled (does it block, show a warning, or fail silently?). Also quote the full settings.json example containing an http hook."}

## HTTP hook handler entry

The page's example for an HTTP hook (from "HTTP hook fields"):

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "http",
            "url": "http://localhost:8080/hooks/pre-tool-use",
            "timeout": 30,
            "headers": {
              "Authorization": "Bearer $MY_TOKEN"
            },
            "allowedEnvVars": ["MY_TOKEN"]
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

The page doesn't show a standalone settings.json file. This is the `hooks` block that would sit inside one.

Field details:

- **`type`** (required): `"http"`.
- **`url`** (required): "URL to send the POST request to."
- **`headers`** (optional): "Additional HTTP headers as key-value pairs. Values support environment variable interpolation using `$VAR_NAME` or `${VAR_NAME}` syntax. Only variables listed in `allowedEnvVars` are resolved."
- **`allowedEnvVars`** (optional): "List of environment variable names that may be interpolated into header values. References to unlisted variables are replaced with empty strings."
- **`timeout`** (common field): Defaults to 600 seconds for HTTP hooks. Claude Code lowers the default to 30 on `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreModelSwitch`, and `PostModelSwitch`, and to 10 on `MessageDisplay`.
- **`statusMessage`** and **`if`** (common fields): A spinner message while the hook runs, and a permission-rule filter for tool events.
- **`onFailure`** (optional): `"continue"` (default) or `"block"`. Requires Claude Code v2.1.295 or later.

## Request body

Yes, it's the same JSON. The page says: "Claude Code sends the hook's JSON input as the POST request body with `Content-Type: application/json`." The input is the same as what command hooks receive on stdin, including the common fields and the event-specific fields.

## Expected response

The response body uses the same JSON output format as command hooks. Per "HTTP response handling":

- **2xx with an empty body**: "success, equivalent to exit code 0 with no output." So a 200 with no body is a success.
- **2xx with a JSON object body**: "parsed using the same JSON output schema as command hooks. A body that fails schema validation is a non-blocking error."
- **2xx with any other body, such as plain text**: "non-blocking error, handled the same as a non-2xx status. Claude Code doesn't add the text to Claude's context."

To block a tool call or deny a permission, return a 2xx with a JSON body containing the appropriate decision fields.

## Errors and failures

By default, failures are non-blocking:

- **Non-2xx status**: non-blocking error.
- **Connection failure**: non-blocking error.
- **Timeout**: the hook is canceled, and its output is discarded.

After a non-blocking error, the action proceeds. On events such as `PreToolUse`, the page says a non-blocking error shows a `<hook name> hook error` notice in the transcript. It doesn't say exactly how HTTP errors are displayed, so that's likely but not confirmed.

To block the action on failure, set `"onFailure": "block"`. The page lists these as failures:

- The connection fails, or the response status isn't 2xx.
- The hook reaches its timeout.
- A 2xx body is neither empty nor a JSON object.

With `"block"`, a failure does what exit code 2 does on that event. The exception is `PermissionRequest`, where it denies the request. The field has no effect on `Stop`, `SubagentStop`, `TaskCompleted`, and `TeammateIdle`.

## Allowlists

Two settings apply to HTTP hooks from every source:

- `allowedHttpHookUrls`: when defined at any settings level, an HTTP hook runs only if its URL matches the merged allowlist.
- `httpHookAllowedEnvVars`: when defined, only the listed variables are interpolated into hook headers.

# yolo-twice engine API (contract v1)

One engine daemon per machine, bound to `127.0.0.1:9656`, serving every registered project.
Runtime state lives in `~/.yolo-twice/engine.json` (`{pid, port, started, version}`) and
`~/.yolo-twice/engine.log`. Per-project data lives in `<project>/.yolo-twice/` (see design.md §5).
Every endpoint that touches a project takes `project=<absolute project root>`; when omitted the
most recently registered project is used. All JSON uses the types from `@yolo-twice/core`
(`Event`, `StructureNode`, `ProjectIndex`, `Config`) and `@yolo-twice/analyzers` (`TextArtifact`, `SearchHit`).

| Method | Path | Body / query | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | `/health` | | `{ ok, version, pid, started, projects: string[] }` |
| GET | `/api/projects` | | `[{ root, slug, name, sessions }]` |
| POST | `/api/projects` | `{ cwd }` | registers the project root of `cwd`, runs an ingest, returns `{ root, slug, name, sessions }` (idempotent) |
| GET | `/api/sessions` | `project` | `ProjectIndex & { current?: string }` where `current` is the session with the latest activity |
| GET | `/api/sessions/:id` | `project` | `{ structure: StructureNode, graph: string, events: number, config: Config }` |
| GET | `/api/sessions/:id/structure` | `project` | `StructureNode`, decorated with cached `text` granularities |
| GET | `/api/sessions/:id/graph` | `project`, `level=1\|2\|3` | `text/plain` mermaid |
| GET | `/api/sessions/:id/events` | `project`, `after=<event id>`, `limit` (default 500) | `{ events: Event[], next?: string }` in append order |
| POST | `/api/sessions/:id/text` | `{ project, node, granularity }` | `TextArtifact` (lazy summarization; computed on demand, cached by hash; may take seconds; falls back to the structural summarizer when the CLI is unavailable, with `analyzer: "structural"`) |
| GET | `/api/sessions/:id/digest` | `project`, `since=<event id>` | `{ since, until, events, text }` "catch me up": summary of everything after `since` |
| GET | `/api/search` | `project`, `q`, `session?`, `limit?` | `{ hits: SearchHit[] }` |
| GET | `/api/config` | `project` | `Config` |
| PUT | `/api/config` | `{ project, attention }` | `Config` (persisted to `.yolo-twice/config.json`, broadcast on the stream) |
| GET | `/api/stream` | `project` | Server-Sent Events, see below |
| POST | `/hook` | Claude Code hook JSON (`session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`, `hook_event_name`, …) | `{}` within 50 ms; ingestion is scheduled, never awaited |
| GET | `/` and `/assets/*` | | the built UI from `packages/ui/dist` when present |

## SSE stream

`GET /api/stream?project=` sends `event: <type>` / `data: <json>` frames:

| event | data | when |
|---|---|---|
| `hello` | `{ project, version }` | on connect |
| `hook` | `{ hook_event_name, session_id }` | every hook received for this project |
| `ingest` | `{ session, appended }` | new events were appended |
| `structure` | `{ session }` | structure.json and graph.mmd were rewritten; clients refetch |
| `semantic` | `{ session, node, granularity, interim }` | a text artifact was written |
| `config` | `Config` | attention changed |
| `ping` | `{}` | every 25 s keep-alive |

## Engine CLI (`yolo-twice`)

```
yolo-twice start [--cwd <dir>] [--port 9656] [--foreground]   start (or reuse) the daemon, register the project, print the UI URL
yolo-twice open  [--cwd <dir>]                                 start if needed and open the browser on the current session
yolo-twice stop                                                stop the daemon
yolo-twice status [--cwd <dir>] [--json]                       engine and project state
yolo-twice index [--cwd <dir>]                                 one-shot ingest + derive, no daemon
yolo-twice mode <micro|attentive|balanced|yolo> [--cwd <dir>]  set the attention detent
yolo-twice hook                                                read a Claude Code hook JSON from stdin and forward it (used by the plugin)
```

`--cwd` defaults to the current directory; the project root is the nearest git root above it.

**What `resume` does**

- `yolo-twice resume [session]` rebuilds a Claude Code transcript from the committed `events.ndjson`: main conversation only, every tool call paired with its result, the parent chain re-linked over the records that survive, redacted text as stored.
- It writes the file to the project's folder under `~/.claude/projects/` and runs `claude --resume <id>`. An existing transcript is never overwritten without `--force`, so running it on the original machine is a no-op.
- From inside Claude Code, `/yolo-twice:yolo-twice resume` prepares the file and prints the command to run in a terminal, since you cannot resume into a running session.

**Short answer:** today bun runs the developer tooling and Node runs the shipped engine and a few build tools. We can drop to one, and bun-only is the cheaper path.

**Where each one is needed now**

- **Bun:** the install relies on bun's `workspace:` protocol in four packages. Five test files import `bun:test`. The UI mock uses `Bun.serve`. The engine source runs directly from TypeScript, and the deck runs through bun because Slidev rejects Node 20.
- **Node:** the engine is built to plain JavaScript so that `npx yolo-twice` works for people without bun, and the plugin launcher prefers that build. `tsc`, Vite and VitePress start with a `node` shebang, so `bun run build` quietly runs them on Node. That is where the "Vite requires Node 20.19+" warning comes from.

**Option 1: bun only (recommended)**

I checked the two things that would block it:

- The UI build runs fully on bun with `bun --bun run build`.
- The engine already runs under bun from source, which is how `bun run engine` works.

What changes:

- Prefix the build tools with `--bun`, so `tsc`, Vite and VitePress no longer touch Node.
- Ship the engine to users as a single executable from `bun build --compile`, attached to GitHub releases per platform. The plugin launcher downloads the one for its platform.

That removes Node for contributors. It also removes every runtime requirement for users: they need only Claude Code and curl. And it closes the open gap where an unpublished npm package makes `npx` return a 404.

The costs are a release workflow with a build per platform, and binaries of roughly 60 to 100 MB each.

**Option 2: Node only**

This is possible, but there's more to rewrite:

- Port the five test files to `node:test` or Vitest.
- Rewrite the mock on Node's HTTP server.
- Move workspaces to pnpm, since npm doesn't support the `workspace:` protocol.
- Run TypeScript source through `tsx`.
- Require Node 22 everywhere, because Slidev and Vite need it.

Users would still need Node installed to run the engine.

I'd go bun-only with compiled binaries. Nothing is changed yet. If you want it, the work is the `--bun` script changes, a release workflow, a simpler launcher, and CONTRIBUTING.md down to one runtime row.
